add.issue.name: Plan: move the event-log hot path (parse, order, time-travel split, timeline index) to a Rust wasm core

edit.description.md:
## Why

Profiled the stress fixture (`source/test/stress`, 20 people, 10 years) at 500k events / 92 MB of JSONL, branch `rust-core`:

| stage (GUI/MCP path, virtual nodes off) | 500k |
|---|---|
| load, parse and order the log | 1.44 s |
| replay (materializeAll) | 0.64 s |
| timeline index, cold | 2.25 s, heap 1.2 GB |
| filing a ticket after the log moved (reload) | 2.25 s |
| peak rss | 1.9 GB |

TUI path (virtual nodes on): replay 2.0 s, a write 2.5 s — that cost is in `children.ts`/`state.ts` (virtual field rebuild), a TS algorithm problem, not a Rust one (see the finding ticket).

Every boot, sync, MCP call after the log moved, time-travel checkout and scrubber open pays "load, parse and order" again. It is a pure function of the log bytes and the most self-contained part of the core, pinned by `event-load.test.ts`, `event-date-utils.test.ts`, `event-payload-schema.test.ts`, `hostile-payload.test.ts`, `unreadable-events.test.ts`, `replay-equivalence.test.ts`, the collab suite.

## Scope (selective)

Port to Rust, behind the existing TS API so no test changes:
1. log file parse: envelope, actor from the file name, corrupt-line quarantine
2. causal ordering (`getSortedEvents`)
3. ULID times, effective times, `splitEventsAtTime`, edge
4. payload validation / decode → `UnreadableEvent`s
5. timeline index (`buildTimelineEntries` + windows)

Not ported: materialization, node repo, state, virtual nodes, sync/git. They stay TS; the store hands them ordered events as JSON.

## Shape

- crate `source/rust/epiq-core` (plain lib, no wasm-bindgen), thin C-ABI wasm facade: bytes in, JSON out. Built with `cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release`; the `.wasm` is base64-embedded into a generated TS module so esbuild, npm and SEA all ship it unchanged.
- TS keeps file listing, vanish/re-list, `logSignature`; it reads bytes and feeds the store.
- store is incremental: a file that only grew re-parses its tail; ordering is always recomputed (a synced event lands mid-order).
- `EPIQ_CORE=js` keeps the TS path for differential tests and as an escape hatch.
- wasm over napi: one artifact, no per-platform `.node`, works in SEA without writing to disk. Parked as a human-input ticket.

## Order

Tickets on this board, top to bottom. Each lands as its own PR with the suites green, incl. `npm run test:collab`.

Related on Default: VCE9WDC (every write re-reads the log), 0RYRKZK (scrub without re-materializing).

add.issue.name: compareEvents orders by localeCompare, so the tiebreak depends on the machine's locale; use code-unit order

edit.description.md:
Part of C3GYH0P.

`event-load.ts` `compareEvents` uses `localeCompare` for the ULID tiebreak and for the stringify fallback. ICU collation is locale-sensitive (case and non-ASCII order differ between locales), so two machines could derive different orders from the same event set for forged or foreign ids — the one thing the architecture forbids. For real ULIDs (uppercase Crockford) code-unit order and ICU agree, so no existing board changes order.

Switch both comparisons to plain `<`/`>` on UTF-16 code units, which is what a Rust byte comparison on the UTF-8 form reproduces for the id alphabet. Regression test: mixed-case and non-ASCII ids order identically under `LANG=C` and `LANG=sv_SE` (assert against a fixed expected order, verified red with `localeCompare` under at least one locale). Land before the Rust ordering so both implementations agree by construction.

add.issue.name: Rust: parse a log file — envelope, actor from the file name, corrupt-line quarantine

edit.description.md:
Part of C3GYH0P. Port of `parsePersistedEventsFile` + `parseEventFileActor` (`event-load.ts`).

Input: file name + bytes. Output: `ReconstructedEvent[]` (envelope `v`, `id: [ulid, refId|null]`, the one payload key kept as raw JSON, `userId`, `userName`) and `UnreadableEvent[]` for `corrupt-line` (`<file>:<line> (invalid JSON)` / envelope message).

Must match: split the base name on the first `.` only; strip the `~pending…` marker from the id segment (`pending-log.ts`); re-uppercase a ULID-shaped id; `unknown` defaults; blank lines skipped; the envelope schema (`v` positive int, id tuple of non-empty string and nullable non-empty string) with the same messages `parsePersistedEnvelope` gives.

Rust unit tests for each rule; the TS suite pins the rest once wired (`event-load.test.ts` dotted / no-dot / empty names, corrupt and truncated lines, ULID case).

add.issue.name: Rust: causal ordering — refId forest, sibling sort, genesis-only roots, orphans, cycles, dedupe

edit.description.md:
Part of C3GYH0P. Port of `getSortedEvents` (`event-load.ts`).

Same algorithm, same result: children grouped by `refId`; siblings by id then by the JSON serialisation of the whole reconstructed event (key order `v, id, <action>, userId, userName` — must serialise exactly as TS `JSON.stringify` does, incl. number and string escaping); iterative DFS; roots = `refId: null` events whose single payload key is `init.workspace`; then orphans (`refId` null or unknown) sorted; then the remainder (cycles) sorted; dedupe by id, first placement wins.

Pinned by `event-load.test.ts` (anchor after ref, sibling ULID order, duplicate ids identical whatever the input order, forged second root after history, smuggled `init.workspace` key, chain longer than the call stack). Add a Rust property test: order is invariant under input permutation.

add.issue.name: Rust: ULID times, effective times, splitEventsAtTime and the edge

edit.description.md:
Part of C3GYH0P. Port of `effectiveEventTimes`, `splitEventsAtTime` (`event-load.ts`) and `toEffectiveUlidTimes` / `clampUlidTime` (`date-utils.ts`).

- `decodeTime`: Crockford base32, 10 time chars, invalid → null (where the TS throws)
- effective times: an id more than `MAX_ULID_AHEAD_MS` past `now` inherits its predecessor's effective time, else the first honest one, all-poisoned passes raw, nulls pass without advancing. `now` is an input from TS, never read in Rust, so a replay is reproducible
- split: unapplied when effective time is null or ≥ target, or the parent is unapplied
- edge: last id of the order, null on empty

Pinned by `event-date-utils.test.ts` and the split cases in `event-load.test.ts`.

add.issue.name: Rust: decode and validate payloads — schema versions, one action key, known actions, required fields

edit.description.md:

Order of checks per event, each producing an `UnreadableEvent` with `reason`, `detail`, `targetNodeId` (best-effort `payload.id`, null when ambiguous): unsupported version (`v<N>`) → not exactly one action key / missing id → unknown action (detail = the action) → required fields per action. `invalid-payload` details: match zod's wording where a test pins it (`unreadable-events.test.ts:130`, `event-load.test.ts`); otherwise `<path>: expected <type>`.

Pinned by `event-payload-schema.test.ts`, `hostile-payload.test.ts`, `unreadable-events.test.ts`.

add.issue.name: Incremental store: re-parse only the tail a file grew by, so a write after a sync stops costing a full reload

edit.description.md:
Part of C3GYH0P. Follows the wiring ticket.

The store keeps parsed events per file keyed by `(name, byte length, first-line hash)`. On the next load: unchanged → reuse; grew with the same prefix → parse the appended bytes only; shrank, renamed (a folded pending log), or a different prefix → drop and re-parse. Ordering, effective times and edge are always recomputed over the full set — a synced event lands mid-order (`timeline-index.ts` header explains why append is wrong).

TS still reads the bytes; it may pass only the tail when the store reports the kept length. The `logSignature` fast path in `boot.ts` is untouched.

Tests: a file that grows by one line, a rewritten file of the same length with different content, a pending log folded into its tracked file, a file that vanishes — each yields exactly what a cold load yields. Done when "filing a ticket after the log moved" at 500k drops from 2.25 s to under 0.5 s in the stress harness, with `test:collab` green.

add.issue.name: Decide: wasm (one artifact) or napi (native speed, one .node per platform) for the Rust core

edit.description.md:
Part of C3GYH0P. Proceeding with wasm; this is the fork.

**wasm** (chosen): `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, one ~300 KB module embedded in the JS bundle; ships unchanged in npm and in all five SEA binaries; no dlopen, nothing written to disk at run time; roughly 1.3–2x slower than native on parse/sort; single-threaded; 4 GB address space (a 960k-event log is 170 MB, fine).

**napi-rs**: native speed and rayon threads, but a `.node` per platform — npm needs per-platform optional packages or a fat tarball, and a SEA binary must extract the `.node` to a temp dir and `process.dlopen` it (noexec tmp, antivirus, signing on macOS). More release surface, more to go wrong for users.

The crate is boundary-free (JSON in/out through one `call`), so a napi facade can be added later without touching the core if wasm proves too slow at 960k. Say so here if you want napi from the start.

add.issue.name: Finding (TS, not Rust): with virtual nodes on, a single write costs 2.5 s at 500k events — children.ts and state.ts rebuild

edit.description.md:

Two halves, measured separately:

1. **Resident store in Rust.** The wasm instance lives as long as the process, so the store keeps, per events dir (one at a time — switching projects drops it), each file's parsed events with the byte length it parsed up to (the last newline) and a hash of those bytes. Those objects are the ones state already retains in `eventLog`, so the map costs its entries, not the events.

add.issue.name: Tie the project id to the state branch, so a checkout without project.json can never mint a second identity for the same board

edit.description.md:
How JQS9XDR happened: `ensureProjectFile` (project-setup.ts) only asks whether `.epiq/project.json` exists in *this checkout*. A checkout without it — a branch from before the file, a clone that lost it, a `git rm` — runs init, mints a fresh ULID, and commits it, even though the state branch already exists on origin with the whole board on it. Nothing ties the id to the branch, and the branch is the identity that matters. It stayed `__epiq_state__` by default here, which is what limited the damage to a directory tug-of-war; an init that also minted a fresh state branch name would have started a second, empty board.

Guards, in order of value:
1. **The state branch carries the id.** Init writes `.epiq/project.json` onto the state branch too; every boot compares the checkout's id with the branch's and fails on a mismatch with a precise message and a repair (`epiq project adopt`, rewriting the checkout's file from the branch). Drift becomes impossible to work under, rather than silent.
2. **Init adopts before it mints.** TUI and MCP init look for the state branch locally and on origin (`git ls-remote --heads origin <stateBranch>`) first; if it exists, the id comes from it. A new id is minted only when no state branch exists anywhere.
3. **Relocation never crosses ids.** `ensureStateBranchWorktree` moves the worktree only when EPIQ_GLOBAL_DIR differs; the same global dir holding the branch under another id's directory is drift, refused with the repair pointed at — today it silently shuffles the directory whenever it is clean.
4. **A change to the id does not get through unnoticed.** The commit-msg hook (check-commit-ref) and CI flag any commit that changes `projectId` unless it matches the state branch's.

Data is not at risk from the drift itself — both ids name one branch — but the old `--force` relocation did destroy unsynced events before K6W24FY-era fixes, and a mismatched stateBranch name would fork the board.

add.issue.name: Decide what a pre-v1.5 author with no registry record is called

edit.description.md:
From reviewing ZFZFW9D (branch `ZFZFW9D-log-file-name`, PR #337). Not a blocker for that merge — the branch is self-consistent — but the two answers it ships disagree, and the disagreement is user-visible.

Since SVYYX5A the contributor registry is the source of truth for display names, and since ZFZFW9D an event carries no name at all. That leaves one population unresolved: somebody who authored events **before v1.5.0 and has not written since**, so `ensureContributorCurrent` never registered them. Their only name anywhere is the sanitized segment of their old log file name.

Six readers resolve that name. They do not agree:

**Fall back to the file name** — `timeline-index.identityFor`, `getBoardContributors`, `getAssignableContributors`, `findEventLogAuthor` (all via `loadActorNames`).

**Fall back to the id** — `formatLogLine` (`source/lib/event/format-log-utils.ts`, the TUI's per-ticket log rows) and `getIssueHistory` (`source/mcp/api/issues.ts`, ticket history in MCP and GUI).

So the same person reads as `alice` in the GUI timeline and as `01KSAYRA4GHEKJP888WFBWBRDD` in the ticket history beside it.

## The options

1. **Leave it, and say so.** The split is arguably principled: name *matching* keeps the fallback because getting it wrong mints a duplicate contributor (the failure `mergeRegistryNames` warns about), while single-event *display* prefers the id because the file-name copy is lowercased and dash-mangled — `claude/oskar` reads as `claude-oskar`, `J. Lampa` as `j.-lampa`. Cost: nothing, but the inconsistency stays and the next reader has to rediscover the reasoning.

2. **Give the display readers the fallback too.** `getIssueHistory` is cheap — it is in `mcp/api`, where the state branch root is in hand. `formatLogLine` is not: it is a display function in `lib/` with no root and no way to reach the events directory, so this means carrying the file-name map in `AppState` and filling it at boot. `bootStateFromEventLog` takes an event array and no root, so that is a signature change across ~8 production call sites.

3. **Backfill the registry.** Write one `create.contributor` per pre-v1.5 author, once, and the registry genuinely becomes the source of truth — every reader agrees by construction and `loadActorNames` can be deleted outright. But it writes events on somebody else's behalf, under a name taken from a sanitized file name, permanently, on every clone. That is a migration with a blast radius well beyond this ticket.

## Recommendation

3 is the only one that actually closes the question, and it is also the one that needs a human to say yes — it mints identity events for other people. 1 is the honest stopgap and costs a comment. 2 buys partial consistency for a real signature change.

add.issue.name: The GUI timeline names contributors from the log, so a rename and a tombstone never reach it

edit.description.md:
From reviewing ZFZFW9D. Not caused by that branch — `NAMING_ACTIONS` is identical on main — and not limited to old boards. This one affects every contributor on every version, which is what makes it worth its own ticket rather than a note on KHT69TD.

`source/mcp/timeline-index.ts` never touches the contributor registry. It rebuilds display names from the log's own events:

```ts
const NAMING_ACTIONS = new Set<EventAction>([
	'create.tag',
	'create.contributor',
	'add.swimlane',
]);
```

`rename.contributor` and `tombstone.contributor` are not there, and `buildNameIndex` only ever calls `names.set`. So the name in a contributor's original `create.contributor` payload stands forever:

- **A rename never shows.** Verified against the branch: create `alice`, rename to `Alice Cooper`, write an event after it — `entries.at(-1).actor.name` is still `alice`.
- **A tombstone never takes effect.** Same shape: the name is still `alice` on events after `tombstone.contributor`. Someone who asked to have their display name removed still has it rendered in the GUI event log.

This reaches the user through `getEventTimeline` (`source/mcp/epiq-time-travel.ts`), which serves the `timeline:get` websocket message — the GUI timeline and event log — and the MCP timeline tool.

## Why it matters now

SVYYX5A made the registry the source of truth for display names and ZFZFW9D finished the job by taking the name off disk entirely. The premise of both is that a rename shows everywhere at once. It does in the TUI, where `formatLogLine` reads `state.contributors[userId]?.name`. It does not in the GUI. So the two surfaces disagree about what a *current* contributor is called, and ZFZFW9D's headline claim is not true where most people will look for it.

It is also the case the ZFZFW9D description opens with — "`tombstone.contributor` cannot currently do what it claims" — half-fixed. The name is out of the file name now, but it is still in a `create.contributor` payload in an append-only log, and this reader shows it.

## The shape of a fix

Adding the two actions to `NAMING_ACTIONS` is not enough: the loop can only `set`, and a tombstone has to *clear*. Tags have the same asymmetry (`tombstone.tag` / `restore.tag`), so whatever is done here should cover them.

The more honest fix is for the timeline to resolve names the way everything else does — through the registry, by id — rather than re-deriving them from raw events. That is the same question KHT69TD asks from the other end, so the two should probably be settled together: if the registry becomes the single resolver, the file-name fallback and this index both go away.

add.issue.name: A re-created contributor keeps the timeline on its old name

edit.description.md:
From a post-merge review of the ZFZFW9D initiative. A bug I introduced in `0499dd43`.

`projectLogNames` tracks `tombstoned` in a `Set` so that `rename.contributor` can be refused on a tombstoned record, matching `node-repo`. It never clears that set on `create.contributor` — but `createContributor` overwrites the record wholesale, with no `tombstoned` field, so the board *is* no longer tombstoned and does take the rename.

Verified against a real boot on `76017d9c`:

```
DIFF tombstone, re-create, rename: board=c projected=b
```

So after `tombstone.contributor` → `create.contributor` → `rename.contributor` for one id, the GUI timeline and event log show the name from the re-create while the board, the TUI and every other reader show the renamed one. Exactly the disagreement 2BPYNWE was filed to remove, in the code that removed it.

## Reachability

Not on one machine: both `assumeActor` and `addIssueAssignee` check the registry before writing `create.contributor`, and a tombstoned contributor is present, so they skip it. It takes two writers — one tombstones somebody while another, whose board has not seen that record, creates them — and the merge orders tombstone before create. That is the ordinary case for this system rather than an exotic one; the architecture note's rule is "never assume a single writer".

## Fix

One line: clear the flag on create, where the board clears it by overwriting.

## Why the differential test did not catch it

It exercises every *action* — 17ZFPPA made sure of that — but coverage of actions is not coverage of orderings, and this needs a specific three-event sequence. A sweep of the six tombstone/create/restore orderings finds this one and no others:

```
DIFF tombstone, re-create, rename
OK   tombstone, re-create only
OK   tombstone twice, then rename
OK   restore, tombstone, restore
OK   restore before any create
OK   tombstone before any create, then create
OK   tag: tombstone, re-create, restore
```

Worth landing that sweep alongside the fix, so the next state added to either side is compared in every order rather than only in the one the fixture happens to use.

add.issue.name: A log line for another board's ticket opens under the board on screen

edit.description.md:
Surfaced while reviewing `TQ3W5RF`'s plan against `main` at `5c7c541d`. Read from the code path, not reproduced in a running GUI — confirm before fixing.

**The path.** The scrubber's All-boards toggle changes what is *fetched*, not just what is drawn: `App.tsx:1317` passes `boardId: allBoards ? undefined : selectedBoardId`, and the flag is persisted (`TimeScrubber.tsx:283`). The log panel then lists whatever the window returned — `useEventLog` filters by series, identity axis, query and ticket narrowing, and by nothing board-shaped (`use-event-log.ts:113-146`). A click resolves through `destinationOf` → `openLogDestination` → `openIssueTab(issueId, tab)`, which defaults `board = boardSlug`, the board on screen (`App.tsx:1072`). So a line belonging to a ticket on another board builds `/board/<board on screen>/issue/<that ticket's ref>`.

**Why it cannot be caught downstream.** The server strips the field that would say which board an event belongs to before the payload leaves: `.map(({board: _board, ...entry}) => entry)` in `getEventTimeline` (`epiq-time-travel.ts:159`). `GuiEventTimelineEntry` has no `board`, so the client cannot tell a foreign line from a local one, cannot mark it, and cannot route it correctly.

**Fix shape, in preference order.** Carry `board` on the timeline entry and route the click to the board that owns the ticket — the project-wide search already opens a ticket on a board other than the one on screen, and `openIssueTab` takes the slug for exactly that (`App.tsx:1072`). Failing that, mark foreign lines inert the way a destination-less line already is, which costs the reader a click that looks live.

Worth settling before `TQ3W5RF` lands: follow mode drives the same pair automatically, so the same mis-route would fire without anyone clicking.

add.issue.comment.md:
Plan review (claude/ferris), read against the code. The mode is well argued; agenda item 1 is not a preference. The timeline loses on four counts, so this half of the review is about the event source. Rest follows in a second comment.

**1. Not scoped to this board.** The fetch passes `boardId: allBoards ? undefined : selectedBoardId` (`App.tsx:1317`), and All-boards is a persisted reader toggle that "changes what is fetched, not just what is drawn" (`TimeScrubber.tsx:283`). With it on the newest event may belong to another board, while `openIssueTab` defaults `board = boardSlug` (`App.tsx:1072`) — follow builds a URL for a foreign ticket under the board on screen. The server strips `board` from every entry (`epiq-time-travel.ts:159`), so the client cannot even detect the case to refuse it. The same pair already mis-routes a *click* today: filed as `S021YSM`, "A log line for another board's ticket opens under the board on screen".

**2. It goes empty.** `events: inWindow.length > TIMELINE_EVENT_CAP ? [] : inWindow`, cap `20_000` (`epiq-time-travel.ts:37,194`). Past it the payload is buckets only and follow silently never fires — no error, no toggle state. This project's own log is at 6656 events, so that is a horizon in this repo.

**3. Ordered by wall clock.** `entries.sort((left, right) => left.t - right.t)` (`timeline-index.ts:435`), over `toEffectiveUlidTimes`, which repairs only times more than 24h ahead (`date-utils.ts:18`). "Newest = max t" is the comparison the architecture rules out, and it bites where this feature lives: a peer clock 10 min fast pins follow and it goes deaf for 10 minutes; a peer 10 min slow lands mid-array, max-t never moves, and follow never fires for them at all. Both silent, and remote writers are the entire use case.

**4. Latency, and an unstated dependency.** While following, this client cannot write — so *every* event it can act on arrives from elsewhere, i.e. from `startGuiAutoSync` (`api-autosync.ts:110`), whose own comment already names "an agent appending to the same worktree". Default interval 15s (`:19`), and only when `autoSync && userName && preferredEditor` (`:60-71`). With autosync off the toggle does nothing at all; it should be unavailable and say why.

So the design receives a `state` broadcast that exists *because* events landed, then spends a second round trip on a window of up to 20k entries to learn what they were. The server holds the before/after `logSignature` and a memoised `getTimelineIndex`, so it can name the new events exactly. That is the websocket protocol, which ships with the build — the "never break old clients" rule is about the log format and does not apply here.

The reuse argument is thinner than stated, too: `destinationOf` takes a `LogEntry` (`event-log.ts:21`), not a `GuiEventTimelineEntry`. What is reused is `tabFor` plus three field reads.

**Whichever source wins, "new" must be a set difference over event ids, never a max over a time axis.** Immune to skew; gives the burst rule for free, because the burst *is* the diff; yields the count of destination-less events agenda item 3 asks about, so the reader can be told rather than silently skipped; and, by seeding the set on enable without navigating, it answers a question the plan never asks — does switching follow on jump you to the current head, or wait for the next event?

add.issue.comment.md:
Review, second half: the read-only mode, persistence, and three smaller things.

**Agenda item 2 is not a fork.** `MUTATING_MESSAGE_TYPES` already classifies every writing message (`gui/client/lib/gui-mutations.ts`) and the *server* imports it (`websocket.ts:65,855`). Wrap `send` (`use-board-socket.ts:67`) once with detach-then-send: that is the specified behaviour, not an interception that lies, and nothing can slip through a control somebody forgot to disarm. Disarm the affordances on top, for honesty — a missed one is then cosmetic rather than a correctness hole. The palette half is one line: `needsWrite` (`command-registry.ts:9`) already answers "can this write" for every command, so add `following` to `CommandContext` beside `scrubbing`. (`sync` is in the mutating set, but the client only sends it from the palette handler at `App.tsx:1514` — there is no client-side autosync — so treating it as a detaching write is safe.)

**"Read-only" is a misnomer, and the test it implies cannot fail.** Nothing is ever refused: a click detaches and *then* writes. The proposed case — the server still accepts a write from elsewhere while one client follows — passes on `main` today, with the feature absent. Worth keeping as a canary, but the property actually under test is "a disarmed click writes exactly once, after detaching". The name also invites the next reader to trust the mode as a safety property, or to reach for `websocket.ts:863` — the trap this ticket already warns about.

**Agenda item 4: do not persist.** Every `usePersistedFlag` today is a view preference — log open, which series show, collapsed, compacted diff, All-boards. Follow would be the first that changes what the board *does* rather than what it shows. Nobody will connect a board that opens disarmed and navigating by itself to a toggle they flipped yesterday.

**Three smaller ones.**

- Navigation is pushed, not replaced (`void navigate(...)`, `App.tsx:1089`). After an hour of following, Back walks the reader through an agent's activity. Follow-driven navigation wants `replace: true`, and `openIssueTab` has no such parameter today — six call sites.
- The third option named in the previous comment, holding the navigation briefly after a reading click, is needed however the "only a write detaches" call goes. Even with no reading click at all, follow takes the board away mid-read whenever an agent is busy. A short quiet period after *any* reader interaction — scroll and hover included — composes with the debounce already planned.
- Where the state lives: a flag, a seen-set, the live/theatre/narrowing gate, the refetch join and the detach wrapper. Five more `useState` in `App.tsx` makes `HZCA9EG` worse. This is a `use-follow-head.ts` owning the whole question and handing out `{following, toggle, disarmed}`.

Nothing here argues against the feature or against the "only a write detaches" call, which I would keep. The one thing I would not build as described is the event source.

add.issue.comment.md:
claude/ferris, on the rewrite. It answers the four counts. Three things the new source does not inherit, and one correction to my own number.

**1. Board scope did not go away with the timeline.** Count 1 had two halves and only the first was about the timeline's fetch. The second is `openIssueTab` defaulting `board = boardSlug` (`App.tsx:1072`), and the `state` broadcast is project-wide — it carries every board. So whatever rides the broadcast has to name the event's board, and follow has to either route there or ignore events off the board on screen. That is a decision for the plan, not something to discover while building. `S021YSM` stays independent as a *click* bug, but follow would reach the same mis-route with nobody clicking.

**2. Three places build a `state` frame, and the one follow depends on is not the obvious one.** `broadcastDerivedState` (`websocket.ts:88`, via `deriveGuiState`, `mcp/api/state.ts:98`), the connect-time `sendGuiState` (`websocket.ts:99`, via `getGuiState`, `:284`), and autosync (`api-autosync.ts:103`, also `getGuiState`). All three funnel through `slimStateResult`, but they are separate call sites, and the outbound frame is typed only as `{type, payload}` (`gui-broadcast.ts:18`) — miss one and nothing fails, it just goes quiet. The one that carries every event this feature exists for is autosync's, which is the one furthest from the socket code.

Related: the new-events field belongs on the *envelope*, beside `payload`, not inside `ApiState`. `ApiState` is the MCP's state shape as well, and GUI follow bookkeeping in `mcp/api` would be a layer crossing for no gain.

**3. Who owns the seen-set.** The description says both "the server names the new events on the broadcast" and "'new' is a set difference over event ids". Those are different owners, and the difference shows up on reconnect: `sendGuiState` on connect carries no diff, and a socket that drops for thirty seconds comes back to a full state with no baseline. A server-side diff is also per-server, not per-follower. Keep the diff on the client — the server may name what it applied as a hint, but the seen-set has to be the follower's, re-seeded on connect and on reconnect *without* navigating, exactly as on enable.

**Correction.** I said this log is at 6656 events; that counted `~pending` files alongside the logs they belong to. The committed figure is 6326. It does not move the argument — still a third of the 20k cap — but the number in my first comment was loose.

add.issue.comment.md:
claude/ferris. The description now covers all three; nothing left that I would change. One addendum, which makes point 6 stronger than either of us argued it.

**There is a fourth producer of a `state` frame, and it is a unicast.** `sendStateAfterMutation` (`websocket.ts:120-124`) sends `{type: 'state', payload}` to the mutating socket alone — not through `broadcastGuiMessage`. So the list for the envelope tightening is four, not three. It is the one site a follower never receives, since a follower does not mutate, but it will fail to compile along with the others when the type is tightened, and that is the point: better it appears in the list than surprises whoever does the tightening.

**What it proves.** After a mutation the server calls `onStateChanged()`, which is wired to `guiAutoSync.queueSync()` and nothing else (`api-server.ts:488`). No broadcast. So a *second GUI client on the same server* — another tab, a colleague on the same host — does not reach a follower directly either; its write arrives only when the autosync pass next broadcasts. I had half-expected that case to be an exception to point 6 and it is not: with autosync off, follow is dead even for two tabs on one server, not merely for MCP agents and remote clones. "Unavailable when autosync is off, and saying why" is exactly right, and worth keeping as written — an implementer testing this with two tabs and autosync off will otherwise conclude the feature is broken.
